summary: Parallel research for the FitTrack rebuild: retatrutide protocol, Calgary NW food data, Crunch gym equipment, iOS PWA push, competitor features

reta.approvalStatus: NOT approved anywhere as of Aug 2026 — investigational only. FDA: no approval; Lilly announced (Jul 23, 2026) it will submit a BLA to FDA in Q1 2027, with review typically 10-12 months, so realistic FDA approval is late 2027/2028 at the earliest (freemedicaljournals.com/blog/retatrutide-fda-approval-status-2026, drugs.com/history/retatrutide.html). Health Canada: as of the Jun 30 2026 update, retatrutide does not even appear on Health Canada's public list of new-drug submissions under review — it hasn't reached step one (glp1prices.ca/blog/retatrutide-canada, glp3planner.com/resources/retatrutide-approved-countries). Current real-world access anywhere (including what the user is doing) is via research-chemical/compounding channels outside any approved, regulated supply chain — CBS News reported doctors prescribing it off-label/investigationally despite no approval (cbsnews.com/projects/2026/experimental-weight-loss-drug/). This is unverified/uncontrolled sourcing by definition; the app should flag this to the user, not treat retatrutide as a normal supplement.
reta.mechanism: Retatrutide (LY3437943) is a single 39-amino-acid peptide, fatty-acid-conjugated for a ~6-day half-life enabling once-weekly dosing, that simultaneously agonizes three receptors: GLP-1R, GIPR, and the glucagon receptor (GCGR) (medical.lilly.com/us/products/answers/what-is-the-mechanism-of-action-of-retatrutide-301926; nature.com/articles/s41421-024-00700-0). GLP-1R agonism drives appetite suppression and delayed gastric emptying — the same mechanism as semaglutide. GIPR agonism contributes to insulin sensitization and, per Lilly's own description, was engineered to be relatively stronger in this molecule while GLP-1R/GCGR activity is comparatively more attenuated. The GCGR (glucagon) component is what differentiates retatrutide from tirzepatide (which has no glucagon activity) and semaglutide: in animal models, glucagon-receptor activation adds an energy-expenditure effect on top of the appetite-suppression from the other two receptors, meaning part of retatrutide's edge over dual/single agonists is plausibly not just "eating less" but modestly higher resting energy use — this same glucagon activity is also the most likely driver of its heart-rate side effect (see side effects). Unverified: exact human energy-expenditure magnitude from the glucagon arm alone has not been isolated in a clean human RCT that I found; treat the "increased energy expenditure" claim as mechanistically plausible from animal data, not as a quantified human effect.

sideEffects.frequency: Strongly dose-dependent. ~14.5% at the 1mg dose (close to the user's actual dose) vs 45.2% at 12mg in the phase 2 trial; relative risk vs placebo was 2.69 at 4mg, 4.27 at 8mg, 4.00 at 12mg. Fast-titration arms (jumping straight to a higher dose) saw nausea as high as 60% at 8mg — starting dose and titration speed matter a lot (pace-cme.org/news/results-of-phase-2-trial-with-gip-glp-1-and-glucagon-receptor-agonist-to-treat-obesity/2456473/).
sideEffects.mitigation: Slow titration (which the user's schedule already does: 1mg x2 weeks, then 1.5mg), small low-fat/low-fiber meals during escalation weeks, stop eating well before feeling full, avoid greasy/heavy food the day of and day after injection.

sideEffects.frequency: Most common adverse events overall in the phase 2 NEJM trial; mostly mild-to-moderate, concentrated in the dose-escalation period and easing at a stable maintenance dose (nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2301972).
sideEffects.mitigation: Hydration, fiber/fluid for constipation, bland food and electrolytes for diarrhea; at his low dose (1-1.5mg) this cluster should be milder than the widely-reported 8-12mg trial experience.

sideEffects.frequency: ~5-10 bpm average increase observed in trials, peaking around week 24 and declining thereafter; higher than tirzepatide (~2-4 bpm) or semaglutide (~1-4 bpm), attributed to the glucagon-receptor component unique to retatrutide (secondnature.io/us/guides/weight-loss-medications/retatrutide-side-effects; PMC12918571 systematic review/meta-analysis). Reported arrhythmia/palpitation rates across phase 2/3 were 2-11% on retatrutide vs ~2% on placebo, none classified as serious in trial data (doctronic.ai/blog/can-retatrutide-cause-heart-palpitations/).
sideEffects.doseRelated: yes — this is dose-dependent and the user's 1-1.5mg dose is far below the 8-12mg doses that produced the reported 5-10bpm figure, so expect a smaller effect, unverified exactly how much smaller since no trial isolated HR change at 1-1.5mg specifically.
sideEffects.mitigation: Track resting heart rate (his app should log it); if resting HR rises meaningfully and stays elevated, or he gets palpitations, that's a flag to raise with a doctor, not to just push through.

sideEffects.frequency: Class effect of rapid, substantial weight loss (any GLP-1-class drug), not retatrutide-specific; risk rises with faster/greater weight loss.
sideEffects.doseRelated: indirect — tied to rate of weight loss, not dose per se
sideEffects.mitigation: At his low dose the rate of loss should be modest (see below), which is protective; still worth knowing right-upper-quadrant pain after fatty meals is a symptom to escalate, not ignore.

reta.leanMassRisk: Two different evidence sources apply, and neither is a perfect match for a 1-1.5mg, 71kg, non-diabetic user, so treat this as directional. (1) Class data across GLP-1/GLP-1-GIP drugs (semaglutide, tirzepatide): lean/fat-free mass has comprised roughly 25-40% of total weight lost in recent trials (mdpi.com/2218-1989/16/6/364; getfitcraft.com/science/glp-1-muscle-loss-research). (2) Retatrutide-specific: a phase 2 DXA substudy in people with type 2 diabetes (different population, different dose arms than his — 0.5/4/8/12mg) found total fat mass fell 4.9% (0.5mg) up to ~23-26% (8-12mg) vs 4.5% on placebo, and reported that lean mass loss as a share of total weight loss was similar to or somewhat better than comparators, not worse (thelancet.com/journals/landia/article/PIIS2213-8587(25)00092-0/abstract; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40609566/). Taking a reasonable midpoint from the broader incretin-class literature: expect roughly 20-30% of his total weight lost to be lean mass by default, WITHOUT resistance training and adequate protein — and that ratio is exactly what's modifiable. A 2025 case-series (n=3) combining semaglutide/tirzepatide with 3-5x/week resistance training and 0.73-1.04 g protein/lb fat-free mass produced lean-tissue changes ranging from -6.9% to +5.8% despite 13-33% total weight loss (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12536186/); a separate 2025 cohort (n=200) pairing GLP-1 therapy with resistance-training education and protein generally >0.36g/lb bodyweight lost ~13% body weight but only ~3% muscle mass over 6 months (davidprotein.com/blogs/the-column/protein-glp1-medications-muscle-preservation). Bottom line for programming the app: lean-mass loss is not fixed by the drug, it is primarily a function of protein intake and resistance-training adherence, both controllable even by a low-commitment user who trains 3x/week.

nutritionGuidance.proteinGperKg: 1.6-2.0 g/kg bodyweight/day (at 71.2kg that's ~114-142g/day). This sits at the upper end of what's cited for resistance-training individuals in a deficit (1.2-1.6g/kg baseline recommendation, up to 2.0g/kg with resistance training per multiple sources including davidprotein.com and roidly.com/2026/03/06/retatrutide-muscle-loss). Given his appetite will be suppressed by the drug and he's already lazy/low-commitment, front-load protein at the start of each meal since he won't have appetite budget left for it later in the day.
nutritionGuidance.deficitAdvice: Do not chase an aggressive deficit on top of the drug's own appetite suppression — the appetite suppression at 1-1.5mg is real but much milder than at trial doses (8-12mg), so a moderate self-imposed deficit (roughly 300-500 kcal/day below maintenance) is reasonable and safer than relying on the drug alone to crash intake. Consuming under ~60-75% of maintenance calories risks muscle being broken down for energy even with adequate protein (uchealth.org/today/nutrition-vital-when-taking-glp-1-weight-loss-drugs/). Needs his TDEE calculated, which needs height and age — not yet supplied, flag for app onboarding.
nutritionGuidance.hydration: GI side effects (nausea/diarrhea/constipation) plus reduced overall food/fluid intake from appetite suppression raise dehydration risk; no specific retatrutide hydration RCT found, general GLP-1-class guidance of steady fluid intake through the day (not chugging large volumes at once, which worsens fullness/nausea) applies.
nutritionGuidance.micronutrients: Not specifically studied for retatrutide at this dose; general GLP-1-class concern is that reduced food volume can push out fiber/micronutrient-dense foods first because the user has limited 'stomach budget' — prioritize whole foods (vegetables, fruit, whole grains) over ultra-processed low-volume calories when appetite allows, per general GLP-1 dietary guidance (mhs.net/blog/2026/03/glp-1-diet-what-to-eat-when-taking-weight-loss-medications). Unverified: no retatrutide-specific micronutrient deficiency data found.
nutritionGuidance.creatine: Reasonable to continue. Creatine monohydrate 3-5g/day is one of the most-studied supplements and an RCT using gold-standard kidney testing found no effect on GFR, creatinine clearance, urea, electrolytes or proteinuria even in resistance-trained adults on high protein — but that finding is sourced through a secondary aggregator (weightlossproviderguide.com/glp-1-and-creatine) here, not the primary RCT, so flag as moderately-verified. No completed study has specifically shown creatine preserves muscle in people on a GLP-1/triple-agonist — its plausible benefit rides on the resistance training and protein doing the actual work, not the creatine itself.

reta.trainingGuidance: Resistance training, not cardio, is the lever that protects lean mass here — the case-series and cohort data above show lean-mass outcomes ranging from meaningful loss to actual gain at similar total weight loss, with resistance-training frequency and protein as the differentiators, not the drug dose (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12536186/). His stated commitment (3x/week, 45-60min at Crunch Fitness) matches the 3-5x/week frequency used in the favorable-outcome case series, so the plan should be built around that, not around adding more days — a 4th "bonus" day is more likely to get skipped and doesn't move the needle enough to justify programming for it given his stated low-commitment profile. Program full-body compound movements (squat/hinge/press/pull pattern each session) over body-part splits, since 3x/week full-body hits each muscle group with enough frequency to signal "keep this tissue" even on a week where one session gets missed — a split gets a muscle group skipped entirely if one day drops. Cardio is optional/secondary: it doesn't preserve lean mass the way resistance training does and competes for the same limited calorie/recovery budget while in a deficit; if used at all, keep it light (walking) rather than adding a real cardio-fatigue cost on top of training + a caloric deficit + a drug that already raises resting heart rate. Unverified: no retatrutide-specific resistance-training RCT completed yet — the cited trial (clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07457437, "Function and Lean Mass Preservation With Resistance Exercise During a GLP-1RA Treatment") is registered but results were not found, so this guidance is extrapolated from GLP-1/tirzepatide-class evidence, not retatrutide-specific evidence.
reta.doseTimingVsTraining: No retatrutide-specific or GLP-1-class data found on optimal injection timing relative to training sessions. General, unverified-for-this-drug practical reasoning: nausea/GI symptoms are usually worst in the 24-48h post-injection and during the first days after a dose increase, so scheduling harder training sessions away from injection day (e.g., inject the day after a training day, not right before one) is a reasonable low-cost heuristic, not an evidence-backed protocol. Flag as a practical suggestion, not a sourced claim.

weekByWeek.appetiteLevel: Mild-moderate suppression typical in week 1; trial 1mg-arm nausea rate was ~14.5%, so GI symptoms possible but usually mild at this dose.
weekByWeek.expect: Little to no visible/scale change expected yet — early GI adjustment week. Do not judge the drug or the plan on week 1 numbers.

weekByWeek.appetiteLevel: Should be settling; less GI symptom load than week 1 typically, though individual variation is real.
weekByWeek.expect: Scale weight may start trending down modestly (data noise dominates at 71kg scale-weight resolution); this is the last week to establish a baseline weekly-average weight before the first dose increase changes the picture.

weekByWeek.appetiteLevel: Expect a step back up in GI symptoms/appetite suppression for a few days after this increase, similar to (smaller than) what trial dose-escalation weeks showed.
weekByWeek.expect: Possible short GI-symptom bump; don't schedule the hardest lift of the week in the 48h right after this specific injection if it can be avoided.

weekByWeek.dose: 1.5mg (2nd week at 1.5mg, per plan a maintenance-style hold)
weekByWeek.appetiteLevel: Should be re-settling toward the milder week-2-at-a-dose pattern seen at 1mg.
weekByWeek.expect: By week 4 overall, the 1mg-arm trial trajectory (-7.2% at 24 weeks, -8.7% at 48 weeks) is the best available anchor, and it front-loads early — but that's a 48-week trial curve, not a 4-week one, so realistically expect only a small, mostly-noise scale change by this point. Do not extrapolate a 4-week trend into a monthly loss rate.

reta.expectedWeightLossRate: Conservative, dose-matched anchor: in the phase 2 NEJM trial, the 1mg arm (closest match to his 1-1.5mg dosing) lost -7.2% of body weight at 24 weeks and -8.7% at 48 weeks vs -1.6%/-2.1% on placebo (search result citing nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2301972, n=69 in the 1mg arm, trial NCT04881760). At his weight (71.2kg) that trajectory maps to roughly 5.1kg by 24 weeks and 6.2kg by 48 weeks IF he tracked the 1mg-arm trial population exactly — he won't exactly, since he's titrating to 1.5mg (slightly higher than the flat-1mg trial arm, so plausibly somewhat faster) but is a real-world user with imperfect adherence and no trial-protocol structure (plausibly slower). Do not promise the widely-quoted 20-30% figures — those come from 8-12mg maintenance doses held for 48-80 weeks in TRIUMPH-1 (up to 28.3% at 80 weeks, 30.3% at 104 weeks per investor.lilly.com/news-releases/news-release-details/lillys-triple-agonist-retatrutide-delivered-powerful-weight-loss and ajmc.com/view/retatrutide-achieves-up-to-30-3-average-weight-loss-in-phase-3-triumph-1-trial) — his dose is roughly 1/8th to 1/6th of that. A realistic weekly rate to program the app around: roughly 0.1-0.25 kg/week on average over the first 2-3 months, front-loaded (faster in weeks 1-8, tapering after), assuming he holds around 1.5mg — NOT the 0.5-1kg+/week sometimes seen anecdotally at high trial doses. Unverified: no trial arm exactly replicates his specific titration schedule (1mg→1.5mg), so this is an extrapolation from the closest available dose-matched data, not a direct citation.
safetyFlags: This is an investigational, unapproved drug (no FDA, no Health Canada approval as of Aug 2026) obtained outside the regulated pharmaceutical supply chain — the app should not present it as a routine supplement; medical supervision (bloodwork, physician check-ins) is appropriate given the lack of regulatory oversight on the product itself.

Persistent or severe abdominal pain, especially right-upper-quadrant pain (possible gallstone), or pain radiating to the back (possible pancreatitis) — stop and seek medical care, this is a known class-wide risk tied to rapid weight loss.

Resting heart rate rising and staying elevated, or new palpitations — retatrutide's glucagon-receptor activity is specifically linked to HR increases (~5-10bpm at trial doses) unlike semaglutide/tirzepatide; worth a baseline HR reading now and periodic checks.

Persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, or signs of dehydration (dizziness, dark urine) — GI side effects that don't resolve after the escalation period warrant dose reassessment, not pushing through.
Height and age are not yet supplied and are required to calculate BMI, TDEE, and set a realistic calorie deficit target — flagged explicitly per the task brief, do not invent these values.

No InBody/DEXA means lean-mass tracking has to be inferred (scale weight trend + progressive-overload performance in the gym as a proxy for "am I losing strength/muscle") rather than measured directly — set that expectation in the app rather than promising body-composition precision the tools don't support.

Rapid/large drops in scale weight (much faster than the ~0.1-0.25kg/week conservative estimate above) at this low a dose would be unusual and worth a gut-check on whether intake has dropped too far (see the 60-75% of maintenance-calories floor above) rather than assumed to be "working extra well."

food.accuracyNotes: CONFIDENCE LEVELS: "published" = pulled from the chain's own nutrition data (via aggregators that mirror it, since brand PDFs repeatedly failed to parse via WebFetch — Popeyes, Church's, and Boston Pizza source PDFs returned binary/unparseable content, so I fell back to third-party aggregators like mynetdiary/fatsecret/fastfoodnutrition.org that cite the brand as source). "chain-equivalent" = a national chain's figures but pulled from an aggregator with some inconsistency across sources (e.g. Dave's Hot Chicken tender calories ranged 490-550 kcal depending on source; Church's chicken breast ranged 200-250 kcal; McDonald's/Mary Brown's items were dropped entirely from the final list because I could only confirm calories, not full macros, and I didn't want to fabricate protein/carb/fat splits). "estimated" = every independent Sage Hill/Beacon Hill/Nolan Hill restaurant (Kolachi, Twist of TAJ, Foodyard, Marhaba, Jaffa, Baladi, Vietnam Palace, Barcelos, Paros, Rice Table, California Thai, Baekjeong, Blowers & Grafton, Bro'Kin Yolk, State & Main) — none publish nutrition, so these are built from typical dish composition (protein weight, oil/ghee load, rice volume) and could be off by 20-30% in either direction, especially fat (South Asian curries are the biggest swing risk since oil quantity varies enormously by kitchen). PORK CAVEAT: Boston Pizza's Clubhouse-style sandwiches and Panago's "True Canadian" pizza default to bacon (pork) — I excluded/flagged those explicitly. Baekjeong Korean BBQ and Blowers & Grafton also sell pork dishes on the same menu; only the specific pork-free items were selected, and ordering must be deliberate (ask "no bacon"). MISSING PROFILE DATA: height and age were not supplied and are required for any TDEE/calorie-target calculation (Mifflin-St Jeor or similar) — flagging this back to the orchestrating agent rather than guessing. Weight (71.20 kg, 2026-08-24) is the only anthropometric fact on record. Marhaba Restaurant's listed address (Westwinds Crescent NE) is genuinely across the city from Sherwood NW, not a short local delivery — kept in the list because search results explicitly named it as serving the Sage Hill/Nolan Hill/Evanston area, but flagged for the consuming agent to verify delivery radius before relying on it. Grocery staple macros are standard USDA/Canadian Nutrient File reference values or read off package labels, not independently lab-verified by me — treat as reliable but not gospel to the decimal place. Home recipe macros are fully self-estimated from standard recipe proportions (no lab source exists for a home-cooked dish) — use them as directional planning numbers, not precise logging.

ios.webPushOnIOS: VERIFIED. Web Push works in an iOS home-screen PWA starting iOS/iPadOS 16.4 (March 2023), and remains current through iOS 26 in 2026. Exact conditions: (1) The site must be added to the Home Screen via Safari's Share sheet > "Add to Home Screen" first. Web Push does NOT work for a page merely open in a Safari tab, only for the installed standalone app. Source: webkit.org/blog/13878/web-push-for-web-apps-on-ios-and-ipados/, corroborated by pushpad.xyz/blog/ios-special-requirements-for-web-push-notifications. (2) The permission prompt (Notification.requestPermission()) can ONLY be triggered by a direct user gesture, a tap on a button inside the already-installed web app. It cannot be requested on page load or automatically. Same webkit.org source, plus median.co/blog/how-to-add-push-notifications-to-your-mobile-website-on-ios-16-4. (3) Once granted, push notifications behave like native app notifications: Lock Screen, Notification Center, paired Apple Watch, Focus Mode filtering, and Badging API support for the home-screen icon badge count. Source: webkit.org/blog/13878. (4) UNVERIFIED: one secondary source seen only as a search snippet (mobiloud.com) claimed Web Push was blocked for EU users under iOS 17.4+ due to DMA browser-engine rules; could not confirm this is still true in 2026 or was reversed. Low relevance since the friends are Calgary-based, flagged for completeness only. (5) Underlying requirement: a registered service worker and a linked manifest.json are prerequisites for the install/push pipeline; standard PWA plumbing, not iOS-specific, but the app must satisfy it before any of the above applies.
ios.addToHomeScreen: VERIFIED, unchanged in 2026, nothing about this can be automated or deep-linked. Flow: user must open the site in Safari specifically. Chrome/Firefox/Edge on iOS are all WebKit-wrapped and lack the "Add to Home Screen" UI, so it only works from Safari. Then: tap the Share icon (square with up arrow) in Safari's toolbar > scroll down and tap "Add to Home Screen" > confirm the name/icon on the preview screen > tap "Add" in the top-right. The icon then appears on the home screen and launches standalone (no Safari chrome) on subsequent taps. There is no automatic install prompt on iOS (unlike Android's beforeinstallprompt), no way to trigger the Add-to-Home-Screen sheet programmatically from JS, and no shareable link that pre-fills the install for a friend, each person must do this manually in Safari on their own device. As of iOS 26, Apple changed default behavior so that any site added to the Home Screen opens as a standalone web app by default even without a manifest, but a manifest.json is still needed for a proper icon/name/theme-color/splash and for install eligibility signals in some contexts. Sources: mobiloud.com/blog/progressive-web-apps-ios (general flow, cross-checked against multiple 2026 PWA guides in search results), apple developer library "Configuring Web Applications" (archived but still the canonical meta-tag reference): developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/AppleApplications/Reference/SafariWebContent/ConfiguringWebApplications/ConfiguringWebApplications.html. Practical implication for this project: the onboarding message to friends must literally say "open this link in Safari, not in Messages' in-app browser, not Chrome" since tapping a link inside Messages/Instagram often opens an in-app browser that does NOT expose the Add to Home Screen option in the same way (UNVERIFIED specifics of which in-app browsers block it in 2026, but this is a well-known long-standing gotcha worth warning about).
ios.safeAreaAndChrome:
VERIFIED core mechanics, some edge cases unverified. Required meta tags for a polished standalone iOS PWA (source: developer.apple.com Supported Meta Tags doc, developer.apple.com/library/iad/documentation/AppleApplications/Reference/SafariHTMLRef/Articles/MetaTags.html, cross-checked with intercom.help/progressier status-bar guide and multiple 2026 PWA guides):
- <meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-capable" content="yes"> : runs full-screen/standalone, no Safari chrome, when launched from home screen.
- <meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style" content="black-translucent"> : options are default (white bar, black text), black (opaque black bar), or black-translucent (status bar overlays your content, letting you paint behind it — this is what modern-looking PWAs use, combined with viewport-fit=cover).
- <meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-title" content="AppName"> : short name shown under the home-screen icon; iOS ignores manifest.json's "name"/"short_name" for this, this meta tag is what controls it (source: multiple docs including the metathis R package doc summarizing Apple's own guidance, cross-checked against gokulkrishh/awesome-meta-and-manifest on GitHub).
- <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover"> : viewport-fit=cover is required to let content extend under the notch/Dynamic Island and home indicator so you can then pad it back with safe-area insets instead of leaving black bars.
- <meta name="format-detection" content="telephone=no"> : stops Safari from auto-linking things that look like phone numbers (annoying in a fitness/food-logging app full of numbers).
- <link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/icon-180.png"> : iOS does NOT read the manifest.json icons array for the home-screen icon, it needs this link tag. 180x180 PNG, no transparency (iOS composites a white background under transparent pixels, so a transparent PNG looks wrong), no rounded corners (iOS masks it automatically). Additional sizes (152, 167, 120) are optional fallbacks for older devices, one 180x180 icon covers all current iPhones. Source: multiple 2026 icon guides (coywolf.com, imagcon.app) cross-checked against Apple's historical device-size table.

Safe-area CSS: use env(safe-area-inset-top/right/bottom/left) via padding, e.g. padding-top: env(safe-area-inset-top); padding-bottom: env(safe-area-inset-bottom); on the outermost layout container, or on fixed headers/footers specifically. Requires viewport-fit=cover to be non-zero; without it, env() insets return 0 in many cases (developer.apple.com/forums/thread/699415, developer.apple.com/forums/thread/716552). UNVERIFIED edge case from the same forum threads: some developers report insets returning 0 in portrait when Safari's own chrome already covers the notch, or resetting when the toolbar is hidden in landscape — this is inconsistent/buggy behavior across iOS versions per multiple bug reports, not a clean guarantee, so test on a real device rather than trusting the simulator.

Height: prefer 100dvh (dynamic viewport height, supported iOS 15.4+) over 100vh for full-bleed layouts, since 100vh in Safari's own browser tab includes space behind the collapsing toolbar and causes jumpy layout; in standalone/home-screen mode 100vh is already correct since there's no Safari chrome. 100dvh has a known "cold start" bug (wrong value on first paint before recalculating) per lukechannings.com/blog/2021-06-09-does-safari-15-fix-the-vh-bug/, so pair it with a resize listener or a min-height fallback for safety. To kill the rubber-band overscroll/bounce feel that reads as "a website, not an app," set html, body { overscroll-behavior-y: none; position: fixed; height: 100dvh; overflow: hidden } with an inner scrollable container, or overscroll-behavior: contain on the scrollable element (broad support, standard CSS, not iOS-specific, no dedicated citation needed beyond MDN).
ios.shortcutsHealthKit: VERIFIED, and the honest answer is NO for true zero-interaction: an Apple Shortcut CANNOT read HealthKit step data and POST it to a URL on a fully silent, unattended daily schedule with zero user interaction, for two independent, compounding reasons: (1) HEALTHKIT ITSELF BLOCKS READS WHILE LOCKED. HealthKit data is stored in Data Protection class "Protected Unless Open"; access is relinquished roughly 10 minutes after the device locks, and health data becomes readable again only after the user re-authenticates (passcode/Face ID/Touch ID) to unlock the device. A background HKObserverQuery can fire while locked but will not return data until unlock; background delivery will not launch the app/Shortcut for new data until the device is unlocked. Source: Apple Developer Forums, developer.apple.com/forums/thread/824819 ("Clarification on HealthKit Background Access While Device is Locked") and developer.apple.com/forums/thread/666899, cross-checked against Apple's own security guide support.apple.com/guide/security/protecting-access-to-users-health-data-sec88be9900f/web. The lone documented exception is HKWorkoutSession, irrelevant to a daily step-count pull. (2) SHORTCUTS PERSONAL AUTOMATIONS FORCE A NOTIFICATION FOR "RUN IMMEDIATELY". Since the iOS 17-era rename ("Run After Confirmation" vs "Run Immediately"), Apple removed the ability to fully silence a Personal Automation: even with "Run Immediately" selected (no confirmation tap needed to start), the OS still fires a system notification announcing the automation ran, specifically so the user always knows something happened on their device — the "Notify When Run" toggle to suppress this does not appear once you pick Run Immediately. Source: matthewcassinelli.com/automations-run-immediately-shortcuts-notifications/. Practical net effect for this project: a Time of Day personal automation set to "Run Immediately" targeting a shortcut that reads steps and POSTs them CAN fire on schedule without a confirmation tap, satisfying "no interaction" in the loosest sense, but (a) it will only actually succeed at reading HealthKit data if the phone happens to be unlocked (or gets unlocked within roughly 10 minutes of the trigger) at that exact time, which for a friend's personal daily routine is not guaranteed, and (b) the user will see a system notification every time it runs, which is not literally silent. UNVERIFIED: whether time-of-day automations that specifically touch HealthKit have any special-cased exemption from the notification requirement; the source found is general to all "Run Immediately" automations and does not call out HealthKit specifically, and Apple has no dedicated documentation page on this interaction that was found. RECOMMENDATION for the app design (not a citation, a design call from this research): do not build the daily-steps import around a guaranteed-silent trigger. Instead, either (a) schedule the automation for a time the friend is realistically already awake and phone-unlocked (e.g., a "when I open X app" or a time trigger a few hours after typical wake time) and accept the occasional missed day, which fits the user's own "must survive missed days" requirement, or (b) have the Shortcut itself, when it does run, just prompt with a native "Ask Each Time" one-tap confirmation rather than fighting for silence, since the phone-unlocked precondition already breaks true zero-interaction. Either way, manual fallback (a text field in the PWA to punch in yesterday's step count) should exist since automatic delivery cannot be guaranteed.
ios.shortcutSharing: VERIFIED, straightforward one-tap flow, well documented and unchanged in 2026. In the Shortcuts app: open the shortcut > tap the "..." (more) or the share/export icon > tap "Copy iCloud Link" (this uploads the shortcut to iCloud and generates a public share URL) > tap "Copy Link" > paste that URL into Messages/email/any share sheet. Source: Apple Support, support.apple.com/guide/shortcuts/share-shortcuts-apdf01f8c054/ios (and the same content mirrored across every regional Apple Support domain, e.g. support.apple.com/en-ca/guide/shortcuts/apdf01f8c054/ios, confirming it is current official guidance). On the recipient's side: tapping the iCloud link opens the Shortcuts app (or a web preview first) showing a description/preview of what the shortcut does and what permissions/actions it uses > they tap "Add Shortcut" (also referred to as "Get Shortcut" in older docs) > it's added to their local Shortcuts library in one tap, no account linking, no App Store step. Optional refinement: the shortcut author can add "Import Questions" before sharing, so the recipient is prompted to fill in personal values (e.g., their own POST endpoint URL, a per-user token) at import time rather than the author hardcoding a value that's wrong for every friend — this is the correct mechanism for distributing one shared shortcut to multiple friends who each need to POST to their own unique row/endpoint. Source: same Apple Support share-shortcuts guide, corroborated by imore.com/how-share-your-shortcuts-others-and-how-add-shared-shortcuts. UNVERIFIED nuance: first-time recipients on a fresh device sometimes get an "Untrusted Shortcut" warning requiring an extra Settings toggle (Settings > Shortcuts > Allow Untrusted Shortcuts) if they've never run a shared shortcut before; this is commonly reported in older iOS versions but no 2026-specific source confirming current exact wording was found in this pass, flagged rather than asserted.
ios.iconAndSplash: VERIFIED. Icon: single <link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/icon-180.png"> at 180x180 PNG covers all current iPhones (iOS composites a white backing under any transparency and auto-applies the rounded-square mask, so ship a flat, opaque, square PNG with no corner rounding baked in). iOS ignores the manifest.json "icons" array entirely for the home-screen icon; only the link tag is read. Splash screens (the "launch image" shown for roughly a second while the app cold-starts from the home screen): iOS/iPadOS does not auto-generate one from the icon or manifest the way Android does; it must be supplied via a set of <link rel="apple-touch-startup-image" href="..." media="..."> tags, one image per exact device-resolution/orientation combination, matched to that device's screen via a CSS media query (width/height/device-pixel-ratio/orientation), because there is no single scalable/vector splash mechanism — this is the most tedious part of "looking native" on iOS and is why most teams use a generator script (e.g. the pwa-asset-generator npm package, referenced across multiple 2026 guides such as github.com/onderceylan/pwa-asset-generator) rather than hand-authoring a dozen-plus image variants. During the splash phase, the status bar color is taken from manifest.json's theme_color, and the background of the rest of the splash screen from manifest.json's background_color, so those two manifest fields matter even though icons/name do not. Source: github.com/kariIT/ios-pwa-splashscreen and developer.apple.com/forums/thread/733490, cross-checked against multiple 2026 PWA icon guides (imagcon.app/pwa-icon-sizes, logofoundry.app/blog/pwa-icon-requirements-safe-areas). Ponytail-appropriate call for a friends-only, low-stakes app: skip the full splash-image matrix (it is real, tedious, and multiplies fast across device sizes) and ship just the 180x180 apple-touch-icon plus theme_color/background_color in the manifest; the app will briefly show a plain white/black flash instead of a custom splash graphic on cold launch, which is a minor cosmetic gap, not a functional one, and not worth a generator dependency for a handful of iPhones. Upgrade to full splash images later only if it visibly bothers someone.
gotchas: localStorage/IndexedDB/service-worker registrations in a plain Safari TAB are subject to a 7-day no-interaction eviction (WebKit's Intelligent Tracking Prevention storage cap); a Home Screen-installed PWA is exempt because it runs outside Safari and has its own separate usage-days counter that resets on actual use of the app, per webkit.org/blog/14403/updates-to-storage-policy/ and cross-checked against support.apple.com/en-om/guide/security. UNVERIFIED: Apple's own docs are not fully explicit/unambiguous on this exemption per multiple developer-forum threads (e.g. developer.apple.com/forums/thread/710157) that report confusion/edge cases, so treat local storage in this app as best-effort persistence, not guaranteed, and do not store anything the friend can't afford to lose (i.e. sync anything important to a real backend, not just localStorage).

In-app browsers (Messages link preview, Instagram, sometimes Gmail) can intercept a shared link and open their own embedded WebKit view instead of full Safari; the Add-to-Home-Screen option may be missing or behave differently there. UNVERIFIED exact 2026 behavior per app, but well-known enough to warn friends explicitly: 'open this link in Safari.'

Web Push requires the notification-permission prompt to originate from a real user tap inside the ALREADY-INSTALLED home-screen app, not the marketing/landing page; a common mistake is asking for permission before the user has even added the app to their home screen, which silently fails. Source: webkit.org/blog/13878.

HealthKit data is unreadable while the phone is locked and for up to ~10 minutes is inaccessible even after locking (Protected Unless Open class); any automation depending on Health data must assume it can silently fail to produce data on a given day if the phone was locked at trigger time. Source: developer.apple.com/forums/thread/824819.

Personal Automations set to 'Run Immediately' still push a system notification every time they fire (Apple removed the ability to fully silence them); design the app's UX to expect this notification exists rather than assuming true silence. Source: matthewcassinelli.com/automations-run-immediately-shortcuts-notifications/.

env(safe-area-inset-*) can return 0px in some iOS versions/orientations even with viewport-fit=cover set, per multiple Apple Developer Forum bug reports (developer.apple.com/forums/thread/699415, /thread/716552); test insets on a real notched/Dynamic-Island device before shipping, don't trust the simulator.

100dvh has a 'cold start' bug where it reports the wrong value on first paint before the browser chrome settles; pair it with a resize/orientation listener or accept a one-frame layout jump. Source: lukechannings.com/blog/2021-06-09-does-safari-15-fix-the-vh-bug/.

iOS ignores manifest.json 'name', 'short_name', and 'icons' for a home-screen-installed PWA; those come from apple-mobile-web-app-title and apple-touch-icon link tags instead. Forgetting this is the single most common cause of a PWA that 'installs' but shows the wrong name/icon on iOS. apps.standoutFeature: Adaptive TDEE: derives actual expenditure from the relationship between logged intake and weight-trend change over time, rather than an age/height/weight formula. Begins updating on day 3, keeps refining through ~30 days.
apps.worthStealing: Steal the concept, not the exact math (undisclosed): weight-trend-vs-intake regression to back out real expenditure instead of a static Mifflin-St Jeor number. This matters a lot here because retatrutide will keep expenditure/appetite in flux — a static TDEE will drift wrong fast.

apps.standoutFeature: Lets the user pick between 4 smoothing methods (7-day SMA, simple exponential, double-exponential, proprietary 'Happy Scale Smoothing') and shows a predicted-goal-date estimate off the trend line.
apps.worthStealing: Offer exactly one good default (EMA) and don't expose the other 3 knobs — this user is low-commitment, a mode picker is friction they'll never touch. Steal the goal-date projection, not the menu.

competitors.predictionPatterns:
Four real, documented approaches, in increasing sophistication:

1. Libra (fully documented, github/support docs) — time-weighted EMA, exact formula:
   smoothingDays = 7 (default, user-adjustable)
   smoothingTime = smoothingDays * msPerDay
   time = currentEntryTimestamp - previousEntryTimestamp
   power = 1 - e^(-time / smoothingTime)
   trend_today = trend_yesterday + power * (weight_today - trend_yesterday)
   Time-weighted so a 3-day gap gets proportionally more "catch-up" pull than a 1-day gap — handles missed days by construction, which fits this user directly.
   Forecast: linear regression over the smoothed trend values inside a rolling window (default 7 days) → slope → project forward, capped at 6 months out. With only 2 trend points, straight linear extrapolation; with 1 point, interpolate trend at window start then extrapolate.
   Source: https://libra-app.eu/support/trend/, https://libra-app.eu/support/forecast/

2. Hacker's Diet / TrendWeight lineage — classic single-parameter EWMA:
   trend_n = alpha * weight_n + (1 - alpha) * trend_(n-1)
   Hacker's Diet recommends alpha = 0.9 for the *smoothed estimate of noise-adjusted current weight* using their particular formulation (their write-up frames it as the complement of what's usually called alpha in other libraries — effectively ~10-day meaningful memory). TrendWeight (open source, github.com/trendweight/trendweight) descends from this lineage; its own README only confirms "moving averages" and does not publish its exact constant in the pages fetched — unverified beyond that.
   Source: https://www.fourmilab.ch/hackdiet/www/hackdiet.html, https://github.com/trendweight/trendweight

3. Happy Scale — proprietary, undisclosed, offers 4 selectable modes (7-day SMA, simple exponential smoothing, double exponential smoothing, "Happy Scale Smoothing"). No formula published. Source: https://happyscale.com/support (unverified beyond feature list)

4. MacroFactor — proprietary and explicitly undisclosed: "a moving average of your weight data that places greater emphasis on more recent weigh-ins," described by MacroFactor itself as similar to but not identical to a standard EMA. Uses linear interpolation to fill gaps. No alpha, no window length published anywhere found. Source: https://help.macrofactorapp.com/en/articles/21-weight-trend, https://www.strongerbyscience.com/macrofactor-algorithms-philosophy/ (this URL blocked WebFetch with 403; only the search snippet was usable — mark as partially unverified)

RECOMMENDATION for this build (my call, not a menu of options): use Libra's exact EMA formula since it is the only one fully specified and open, with alpha effectively derived from a 7-day smoothingDays constant rather than a bare fixed alpha — that time-weighting is the right behavior for a "lazy, low-commitment" user who will skip days, since a fixed-alpha EWMA silently under-corrects after a gap while Libra's time-weighted version doesn't. Forecast by linear regression on the last ~14-21 days of trend values (longer than Libra's default 7, because retatrutide dosing changes every 7 days and a 7-day regression window would be mostly one dose-level) and only start showing a forecast/trend line once at least 4 weigh-ins exist over at least 5 distinct days — MacroFactor's own copy is vague on a firm minimum, so this threshold is my own reasonable default, flagged as a design choice not a sourced number.

Retatrutide-specific caveat, unverified by any of the above apps but real and worth building for: rapid GLP-1/GIP-driven loss can include meaningful lean mass loss (cited 25-40% of lost weight can be lean tissue in trial data, per Healthline/clinical summaries below) — the trend/forecast tab should not imply all projected loss is fat, and should surface a protein-target reminder rather than pure calorie-deficit framing. Source: https://www.healthline.com/health/drugs/tracking-weight-loss-on-glp-1s, https://meagain.com/glp-1-muscle-loss
competitors.onboardingPatterns:
Order that works, synthesized from MacroFactor and MyFitnessPal (Noom's is longer/psychology-heavy and not a fit for a "make the call, don't ask" low-commitment user):

1. Goal direction (lose fat / maintain / gain) — MyFitnessPal leads with this, single tap.
2. Anthropometrics needed for any formula (height, age, sex, current weight) — MacroFactor collects these before showing any target. THIS IS THE FLAGGED GAP: user has not supplied height or age. Do not invent them — the app cannot compute an initial BMR/TDEE estimate (Mifflin-St Jeor or equivalent) without both. Ask the user directly before building the onboarding screen.
3. Activity/lifestyle level and training frequency — user already gave this (Crunch Fitness, 3x/week, 45-60 min), reuse it rather than re-asking.
4. Rate-of-change preference — MacroFactor asks the user to pick a target rate (e.g., "aim to lose 1 lb/week") and derives the calorie target as expenditure_estimate - deficit_for_that_rate. Source: https://help.macrofactorapp.com/en/articles/206-what-should-i-do-if-my-initial-expenditure-or-recommended-energy-intake-seems-too-high-or-too-low
5. Weigh-in frequency and coaching-style preference — MacroFactor asks this explicitly rather than assuming daily.
6. Output: an initial calorie/macro target computed from a standard formula (population-average, openly acknowledged as rough), explicitly framed as provisional until 2+ weeks of real data recalibrates it via the adaptive algorithm.

MyFitnessPal's onboarding is shorter and was reviewer-praised specifically for being short: goal, current weight, target weight, activity level, rate of change — done. Source: search snippet from nutrola.app comparison (unverified beyond snippet, treat as directional not exact).

Recommendation for this build: MyFitnessPal-length questionnaire (5-6 questions, under 60 seconds) producing a MacroFactor-style provisional target that explicitly says "this will adjust as you log" — never present the first number as final. Given this user is on retatrutide with a real titration schedule already known (1mg Aug 24, 1mg Aug 31, 1.5mg Sep 7, 1.5mg Sep 14), the onboarding should also capture GLP-1 usage and current dose so appetite-driven low intake days aren't misread as under-eating relative to a target that assumes no medication.
competitors.loggingShortcuts:
Three concrete patterns, cited to Hevy/Strong/Boostcamp:

1. "Log this exercise" one-tap: pre-fill each set's weight/reps with the exact value logged last time for that same exercise (Hevy's PREVIOUS column) — tapping the previous value copies it straight into the active set with zero typing. This is the highest-leverage single feature for a lazy logger: most gym sets are identical to last week's, so most logging becomes tap-tap-tap-done. Source: https://www.hevyapp.com/features/track-exercises/

2. "Log whole session" one-tap: copy an entire previous workout as the starting point for today's session (Hevy: from Profile tab), or save any workout as a reusable routine/template you can start with one tap (Hevy's "Save as Routine"; Strong's templates - tap template, "start workout," fully pre-populated). Source: https://www.hevyapp.com/use-cases/exercise-log/, search snippet on Strong templates

3. Tap-budget as a hard design constraint: Strong gets from cold-open to a logged set in 3 taps once inside an active session, auto-starts the rest timer on log so there's no separate "start timer" action. Boostcamp requires zero setup wizard — a first-time user can be logging within 5 steps of installing. Source: search snippets, repreturn.com and Boostcamp reviews (moderately confident, not primary-sourced screenshots — treat exact tap counts as approximate, not verified against the live app)

Recommendation: build both "repeat last set" (per-exercise) and "repeat last full session" (one tap) as first-class actions on the log screen, not buried in a menu — and default every new set's fields to last time's numbers rather than blank, since blank fields are the friction that kills low-commitment logging.
competitors.adherenceHandling:
Grounded in a real 2026 study on fitness-app harm plus the "never miss twice" behavioral literature, not a single vendor's copy:

- Streak counters as commonly implemented are actively counterproductive: a broken streak triggers a "well I've already failed" thought that predicts giving up rather than resuming, and users report avoiding opening the app specifically to not see a broken streak or a missed-day reminder. Source: https://networkcultures.org/blog/2026/01/19/baby-please-dont-break-the-streak/, https://ogamic.com/blog/streak-anxiety-from-fitness-apps
- A peer-reviewed-adjacent 2026 study found guilt/shame from missed-target notifications led some users to stop logging entirely or to over-exercise to "compensate" for a lapse — both are worse outcomes than just missing a day. Source: https://www.insideprecisionmedicine.com/topics/precision-medicine/fitness-apps-can-have-a-negative-impact-on-users/
- The fix pattern that keeps showing up across sources: replace daily streaks with weekly/rolling-window goals ("3 sessions this week," "any movement counts"), so one missed day doesn't zero out visible progress; and design the "you missed a day" state to say nothing evaluative at all — no banner, no red counter, no "don't break your streak" copy — just show the next actionable step (today's plan) as if nothing happened. Source: https://ogamic.com/blog/why-fitness-apps-make-consistency-harder (mirrored at getgainstrong.com), James Clear's "never miss twice" framing per https://ogamic.com/blog/never-miss-twice-rule-for-working-out

Applied to this user's explicit instruction ("never be optimistic, I am lazy and low commitment"): the app should never say anything falsely upbeat ("You've got this!") on a miss, but it should also not editorialize negatively — the honest, non-preachy move is silence plus the next concrete action. Weekly totals (workouts done / 3 planned, weigh-ins logged / target) rather than a daily streak number. If 2+ days are missed, the only message the research supports is a neutral one-line nudge with zero guilt framing, not a warning, not encouragement — just state the fact ("2 sessions left this week to hit 3") and move on.
antiPatterns: Daily all-or-nothing streak counters — documented to cause the exact disengagement they're meant to prevent (source: networkcultures.org, ogamic.com above).

Guilt-framed or falsely-upbeat push notifications on a missed log day — explicitly barred by this user's own instruction and independently linked to users abandoning tracking altogether (insideprecisionmedicine.com).
Exposing 4 different smoothing-mode toggles like Happy Scale — a low-commitment user will never configure it; ship one good default.
Forecasting off raw scale weight instead of the smoothed trend (Libra explicitly avoids this because it makes forecasts jump on a single bad reading).
A long Noom-style psychology questionnaire at onboarding — too much friction for a self-described lazy user; MyFitnessPal's short version is the better fit.

Presenting the day-1 calorie/macro target as final rather than provisional — MacroFactor explicitly frames it as a rough starting point pending 2 weeks of real adaptive data; presenting it as authoritative sets up a false sense of precision.

Treating all GLP-1-era weight loss as fat loss in the trend UI — unverified-by-competitor-apps but clinically real risk (up to 25-40% lean mass per cited trial summaries) that this build should account for even though no reviewed competitor app explicitly solves it well.

gotchas: Free-tier Cron Trigger CPU budget is 10ms per invocation (not 10 seconds) — confirmed on developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/. ECDSA JWT signing plus a handful of KV reads is fine for one user; do not scale this design to many users without moving to Paid (30s/15min CPU) or batching sends across multiple ticks.

Cron Trigger limit (5 on Free) is per ACCOUNT, not per Worker — several blog posts (cronuru.com, runhooks.app) state different numbers or imply per-worker; the CF docs page is the source of truth and was fetched directly to confirm this.
Workers KV is eventually consistent (writes can take up to 60s to reach other edge locations) — irrelevant at single-user write volume but worth knowing if this ever becomes multi-writer.

iOS Web Push requires the site be added to the Home Screen via Safari's Share sheet first — an ordinary Safari tab has no Push API at all, regardless of iOS version. Minimum iOS version is 16.4 (March 2023). Notification.requestPermission() must be called synchronously inside a user-gesture handler on iOS or it silently fails.

iOS Safari has no silent/data-only push — every push you send MUST result in a visible notification via showNotification(), or the OS can revoke permission after repeated silent-looking pushes. Don't use push as a background-sync-only mechanism on iOS.

410 Gone = subscription expired or user unsubscribed; 404 Not Found = the endpoint URL itself is invalid. Both mean: delete the push:sub:{userId} KV record immediately on receiving that status from the push service, or you'll keep failing sends into the void and risk the push service starting to rate-limit your VAPID key at scale (irrelevant risk at n=1, but the delete-on-410/404 handling is still correct practice).

The pushsubscriptionchange service worker event exists to let you proactively refresh a subscription before it expires, but it's not reliably fired across browsers/spec implementations — treat 410-triggered cleanup on send as the actual source of truth, not pushsubscriptionchange.

Payload size caps: ~4KB is the practical ceiling most push services (Chrome/Firefox/Edge) enforce; Safari's web push is commonly cited around 2KB. Keep any encrypted payload body small, or skip payload encryption entirely and send tickle pushes (see ponytail note in vapidFlow).

VAPID JWT 'exp' claim must be <= 24 hours from now per RFC 8292; going over doesn't always error immediately on some push services (see github.com/mozilla-services/autopush/issues/794) but is spec-non-compliant and other services will reject it — just always set exp to something like now+12h.

crypto.subtle.sign for ECDSA returns raw IEEE P1363 (r||s, 64 bytes for P-256) directly — this happens to be exactly the JWS ES256 wire format, so no DER conversion step is needed in a Workers/browser implementation. This trips people up when porting Node.js code, because Node's built-in crypto module (not Web Crypto) defaults to DER-encoded ECDSA signatures and needs an explicit dsaEncoding:'ieee-p1363' option to match.

Height and age were not supplied for this user and were not invented — flagging per instructions: any calorie/TDEE/macro target math for the fat-loss + muscle goal needs those two inputs before it can be computed; do not proceed with BMR/TDEE formulas using assumed values.
push.freeTierLimits: Cloudflare Workers Free plan (confirmed against developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/ and /workers/platform/pricing/, 2026): 100,000 requests/day; 10ms CPU time per invocation (same figure applies to Cron Trigger invocations); 50 subrequests per invocation; 5 Cron Triggers per account. Workers KV Free plan: 100,000 reads/day, 1,000 writes/day, 1,000 deletes/day, 1,000 list operations/day, 1GB total storage, all resetting daily at UTC 00:00. All of these are hard caps on Free — requests over the cap fail rather than throttle or queue (per basekv.com/articles/cloudflare-workers-kv-limits-2026, cross-checked against the official pricing page). At single-user, low-frequency-reminder scale, none of these are binding except the 10ms CPU/invocation figure, which is worth designing around from day one (keep the scheduled() handler doing O(few) KV reads and a single JWT sign per tick, not a loop over many users).

refutedClaims.claim: Heart rate side effect entry: "~5-10 bpm average increase observed in trials, peaking around week 24"
refutedClaims.correctValue: Multiple independent secondary sources reporting on the NEJM phase 2 data give ~5-7 bpm at the highest doses (8mg/12mg), with one source citing a specific 6.7 bpm increase at 12mg vs 0.9 bpm on placebo. No source found supports a 10 bpm figure at any dose.
refutedClaims.source: boltpharmacy.co.uk 'Retatrutide Heart Rate Increase' guide (aggregating NEJM 2301972 phase 2 data); helloregimen.com cardiovascular-effects page
refutedClaims.why: The claims doc's own upper bound (10 bpm) is not found in any source I could locate, even ones summarizing the highest (12mg) dose — a dose 8x the user's actual 1-1.5mg. This looks like a rounded-up overstatement, not a fabricated number, but it should be tightened to 5-7 bpm at trial's highest doses and explicitly caveated as unmeasured at 1-1.5mg (which the doc partially does).

refutedClaims.claim: leanMassRisk: retatrutide DXA substudy "reported that lean mass loss as a share of total weight loss was similar to or somewhat better than comparators, not worse"
refutedClaims.correctValue: Secondary sources characterize the finding as lean mass loss being 'comparable to other obesity treatments' / retatrutide 'didn't lose more muscle than other drugs' — i.e. parity, not superiority. One aggregator computed a ~35.4% lean-mass share of total weight loss (from a 64.6% pooled fat-loss-index across 4/8/12mg), which sits at the higher end of the 25-40% class range the doc itself cites elsewhere, not toward the better end.
refutedClaims.source: rethinkpeptides.com summary of Coskun et al. 2025 (Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, PMID 40609566); springermedicine.com summary
refutedClaims.why: "somewhat better than comparators" is not supported by any source found — the actual language in circulation is parity ("comparable"/"similar"), and the one numeric estimate available (~35.4% lean share) is at the upper end, not the favorable end, of the class range. This should be softened to "similar to / not clearly worse than comparators" rather than implying an advantage.

unverifiable: Exact relative-risk multipliers for nausea by dose (2.69x at 4mg, 4.27x at 8mg, 4.00x at 12mg vs placebo) — the underlying nausea percentages (14.5% @1mg, 45.2% @12mg, 60% fast-titration @8mg) were independently confirmed, but the specific RR figures could not be confirmed against a primary source (NEJM full text is paywalled; the cited pace-cme.org page did not contain dose-specific nausea numbers when fetched).

FDA review length of '10-12 months' post-BLA-acceptance — one synthesis source instead suggested ~60 days to accept the filing plus 6-10 months of review, which is a narrower/faster window than the doc's '10-12 months'; standard (non-priority) PDUFA review is nominally 10 months, so the doc's figure is defensible but not independently pinned down to a single authoritative number.

Tirzepatide (~2-4 bpm) and semaglutide (~1-4 bpm) heart-rate comparator figures cited alongside the retatrutide number — plausible and consistent with general knowledge of those trials' cardiac safety data, but not independently re-verified in this pass.

The specific 'expected weight loss rate at 1-1.5mg' figure the app would show the user — the weekByWeek section of the claims JSON was truncated before any quantitative weight-loss-% figure appeared, so there was nothing concrete to check it against. For reference, the phase 2 trial's actual 1mg arm (not titrated to 1.5mg) produced −7.2% least-squares-mean weight loss at 24 weeks and −8.7% at 48 weeks vs −2.1% on placebo — use this as the grounding number if/when the full doc states one.

2-11% arrhythmia/palpitation rate range and the 'none classified as serious in trial data' characterization — plausible given the broader safety profile described elsewhere, but not independently re-confirmed against a primary source in this pass.

Human-isolated glucagon-driven energy-expenditure magnitude — the doc already correctly flags this as unverified/animal-data-only; I found nothing in this pass to override that caveat, so it stands as unverified rather than refuted.
corrections: Nausea-by-dose numbers (14.5% at 1mg, 45.2% at 12mg, 60% fast-titration at 8mg) are CONFIRMED accurate against an independent secondary source reporting the same phase 2 figures verbatim (28/62 at 12mg, 21/35 in the fast-titration 8mg arm) — no correction needed.

Regulatory status is CONFIRMED accurate on all points: no approval anywhere as of Aug 2026, Lilly targeting a Q1 2027 BLA submission, and Health Canada's public new-drug-submission list not showing retatrutide as of the June 30, 2026 update (independently corroborated by a Lilly spokesperson telling Medscape in June 2026 that retatrutide 'has not been approved anywhere in the world'). No correction needed.

Mechanism claims (GIPR ~8.9x more potent than native GIP, GLP-1R ~0.4x and GCGR ~0.3x less potent than native hormones vs endogenous ligands, ~6-day half-life enabling weekly dosing, 39-amino-acid fatty-acid-conjugated peptide) are CONFIRMED accurate against Lilly's own medical-affairs page and the Cell Discovery structural-biology paper. No correction needed.

The CBS News off-label-prescribing claim is CONFIRMED accurate and if anything understates the scale: CBS's investigation found 120+ websites and 50+ clinics staffed by licensed clinicians promoting unapproved retatrutide, plus a 265% surge in Poison Center exposure reports in early 2026. No correction needed, could arguably be strengthened.

DXA substudy fat-mass-reduction figures (4.9% at 0.5mg, ~23-26% at 8-12mg vs 4.5% placebo) are CONFIRMED close to the primary Lancet substudy's reported 4.9% (0.5mg), 26.1% (8mg pooled), and 23.2% (12mg). No correction needed. This substudy also correctly excluded 1mg/1.5mg dose arms, exactly as the doc caveats.

The protein target of 1.6-2.0 g/kg is within the range supported by resistance-training-in-a-deficit sports-nutrition literature (general GLP-1 guidance clusters lower, around 1.2-1.6 g/kg, with up to ~2.0-2.2 g/kg cited for resistance-trained individuals in a deficit) — this is a defensible, non-overstated choice given the doc's own hedging, not a fabricated number.
Soften 'peaking around week 24... ~5-10 bpm' to '~5-7 bpm at the highest trial doses, peaking around week 24' — no source supports the 10 bpm upper bound.

Soften 'lean mass loss ... similar to or somewhat better than comparators, not worse' to 'similar to / not clearly worse than comparators' — no source found frames retatrutide as outperforming comparators on this metric, only as being on par.
retatrutide.verdict: Largely holds up. No invented trial numbers were found: the dosing/nausea percentages (14.5% at 1mg, 45.2% at 12mg, 60% fast-titration at 8mg), the DXA fat-mass percentages by dose, the mechanism/potency figures, and the full regulatory-status section (FDA non-approval, Q1 2027 BLA target, Health Canada absence as of June 30 2026, CBS News off-label-prescribing reporting) all check out against independent secondary sources consistent with the primary literature. Two claims are mild overstatements rather than fabrications and should be tightened: the heart-rate side effect's upper bound of '~10 bpm' (sources top out around 5-7 bpm even at the highest 12mg dose), and the framing that retatrutide's lean-mass-loss share is 'similar to or somewhat better than' comparators (sources support parity, i.e. 'similar to/not worse than,' not superiority). The protein g/kg recommendation (1.6-2.0 g/kg) is defensible, not overstated, given it's explicitly framed as the upper end of a resistance-training-in-deficit range. Several secondary specifics — exact RR multipliers for nausea, the precise FDA review-month count, and the tirzepatide/semaglutide heart-rate comparator figures — could not be independently pinned to a primary source in this pass and should be treated as lower-confidence until checked against NEJM/FDA primary text directly. No evidence found that the regulatory-status claim is wrong in either direction (not overstated toward 'basically approved,' not understated toward 'banned') — it accurately frames retatrutide as investigational-only with real-world access happening through unregulated/compounding channels, which is the correct signal for the app to flag to the user.
